lessons.title: Why Startups Raise Money and When They Should Not

children.text: Every week, some Indian founder announces a seed round on LinkedIn with a photo of the team and a string of celebration emojis. Almost nobody posts when the money runs out. Raising money is not an achievement. It is a trade: you sell part of your company, and part of your freedom, in exchange for cash that lets you move faster. This lesson shows you when that trade makes sense, when it does not, and how to tell the difference, whether you are the founder, the finance person building the runway model or the employee holding ESOPs.

body.text: Funding is fuel, not a finish line. Raise when money will buy growth the business cannot buy on its own. Raise for any other reason and you pay for it with ownership you will never get back.

children.text: What Outside Money Actually Buys

markDefs.definition: How much more cash a company spends than it brings in each month. Net burn = monthly cash expenses minus monthly cash revenue.
The number of months a company can keep operating before its cash runs out, at its current net burn.

children.text: A startup has to spend cash before it earns cash. Salaries, servers, inventory and marketing are paid today. Revenue arrives later, if it arrives at all. The size of that gap is captured by two numbers every founder and finance team must know cold:
burn rate
and
runway

body.caption: The single most important number in an early-stage startup

children.text: Take a Bengaluru B2B software startup with ₹3 crore in the bank that spends ₹25 lakh a month more than it earns. Its runway is ₹300 lakh ÷ ₹25 lakh = 12 months. Now the founders hire six engineers and a sales lead, and net burn rises to ₹40 lakh a month. Same bank balance, but runway drops to 7.5 months. Outside money exists to extend that line long enough for the business to become something investors, or customers, will pay more for.

body.text: A fundraise commonly takes three to six months from the first pitch to money in the bank, and it can take longer when markets are cautious. A startup with six months of runway that is only now starting to raise is already late. Founders who raise well start when they still have 12 to 18 months of cash left.

body.title: Calculate the runway
body.prompt: A Pune edtech startup has ₹4.8 crore in the bank. It earns ₹30 lakh a month in revenue and spends ₹70 lakh a month. How many months of runway does it have?
body.explanation: Net burn is ₹70 lakh minus ₹30 lakh = ₹40 lakh a month. Runway is ₹480 lakh ÷ ₹40 lakh = 12 months. Always divide by net burn, not total expenses. Using ₹70 lakh would wrongly give about 6.9 months.

children.text: Good Reasons to Raise

The test is simple: will this money buy something the business genuinely cannot get from its own cash flow, and is that something worth far more than the ownership you give up? Four situations usually pass.

body.caption: When raising outside capital makes sense

cells: Growth is limited by cash, not demand
Customers want more than you can supply, and each rupee spent on growth reliably returns more than a rupee
A D2C snacks brand that sells out every production batch within days
The market rewards speed and scale
Network effects or winner-take-most dynamics, where being second in a city can mean being irrelevant
Quick commerce players like Zepto, Blinkit and Swiggy Instamart racing to open dark stores
Years of R&D, certification or manufacturing set-up before the first sale
An EV battery or drone company building and testing hardware
Hiring ahead of revenue with long sales cycles
Enterprise customers take 6 to 12 months to sign, so the sales team must be paid long before the contracts land
A Chennai SaaS company selling to mid-sized US businesses

children.text: Bad Reasons to Raise
Because everyone else is raising.
A competitor's funding announcement is not a business plan. Their model, burn and market may look nothing like yours.

markDefs.definition: The point at which a product clearly satisfies a real market need: customers buy, come back and recommend it without heavy pushing.

children.text: To find
product-market fit
by spending.
Money amplifies whatever is already happening. If customers love the product, money helps you reach more of them. If they do not, money just helps you lose it faster.
For validation.
A famous VC logo on your deck feels like proof. The only real proof is paying customers.
Because the valuation offered is flattering.
A high valuation sets a bar the next round must clear. Miss it and you face a down round, which hurts founders, employees and early investors alike.
To avoid fixing the business.
If every order loses money, raising more only postpones the reckoning and makes it bigger.
The Real Price of Outside Money
Equity money has no interest rate and no EMI, so it is easy to think of it as free. It is the most expensive money a successful company will ever take. The bill comes in four parts.

stats.label: Ownership
stats.context: A common range sold in seed and Series A rounds

stats.label: Control
stats.context: Investors gain a say on budgets, hiring, new rounds and exits

stats.label: Expectations
stats.context: Investors need a large outcome, not a steady small business

stats.label: Time
stats.context: VC funds typically run 8 to 10 years and must return cash to their own investors

markDefs.definition: The fall in an existing shareholder's ownership percentage when the company issues new shares to someone else.

children.text: The ownership cost is the one founders underestimate most, because
dilution

is priced at today's value but paid at tomorrow's. Suppose founders sell 20% of their company for ₹2 crore, valuing it at ₹10 crore after the money comes in. Years later, the company is acquired for ₹200 crore. Ignoring later rounds for simplicity, here is what that ₹2 crore really cost:

body.latex: \text{Value of stake sold at exit} = 20\% \times 200\text{ crore} = 40\text{ crore}
body.caption: ₹2 crore raised, ₹40 crore of exit value given up

children.text: That is a brilliant trade if the ₹2 crore is what made the ₹200 crore outcome possible. It is a terrible trade if the business would have got there anyway on its own cash flow.

body.title: What did the money really cost?
body.prompt: A Jaipur handicrafts marketplace sells 15% of the company for ₹1.5 crore. Six years later it is acquired for ₹120 crore. Ignoring any later rounds, what is the 15% stake worth at exit, in ₹ crore?
body.explanation: 15% × ₹120 crore = ₹18 crore. The founders gave up ₹18 crore of exit value for ₹1.5 crore of capital, 12 times what they raised. Whether that was worth it depends entirely on whether the company could have reached ₹120 crore without the money.

children.text: Two Indian Paths: Zerodha and Dunzo

columns.label: Zerodha (bootstrapped)
points: Founded in 2010 by Nithin and Nikhil Kamath
A low-cost discount broking model that generated cash early
Grew largely through word of mouth instead of paid marketing
Reported a net profit of about ₹4,700 crore for FY2023-24
Founders kept full control over pace and direction

columns.label: Dunzo (heavily funded)
points: Bengaluru hyperlocal delivery startup founded in 2014
Backed by Google in 2017, and later by Reliance Retail, which led a $200 million round in 2022
Spent heavily to compete in the fast delivery race
Reported layoffs and delayed salaries from 2023 as fresh funding dried up
Showed that capital raised is not the same as a business that works

body.text: Do not take the wrong lesson from this. Bootstrapping is not always right and raising is not always wrong. Zoho also grew past $1 billion in annual revenue without venture capital, while Zomato used venture capital to build a business that listed on NSE and BSE in 2021. The business model should decide the funding path, never the founder's ego or the market mood.

body.title: A quick test: is your startup default alive or default dead?

children.text: Ask one question: if revenue keeps growing at its current rate and expenses stay flat, will the company turn profitable before the cash runs out? If yes, it is default alive and raising is a choice. If no, it is default dead and raising is a necessity, which is the weakest position to negotiate from.
Example: a startup has ₹2 crore in cash, ₹20 lakh of monthly revenue and flat expenses of ₹40 lakh a month.
Growing 10% a month:
revenue crosses ₹40 lakh in month 9. Total burn before that is about ₹91 lakh, well within ₹2 crore. Default alive.
Growing 3% a month:
revenue takes about two years to reach ₹40 lakh, and total burn along the way is roughly ₹2.7 crore, more than the company has. Default dead.
Same cash, same costs, same starting revenue. The growth rate alone decides whether the founders raise from strength or from desperation.
Why This Matters If You Are Not the Founder

Funding decisions shape everyone's working life at a startup. A fresh round usually means aggressive hiring, bigger budgets and generous ESOP grants. A shrinking runway usually means hiring freezes, delayed increments and, at worst, layoffs. HR teams plan headcount around the runway. Treasury and finance teams build the cash forecast that decides when the founders must start raising. And every employee holding ESOPs owns a piece of the outcome. You do not need to be in the boardroom to read the signals.

body.title: Questions worth asking about your own startup
steps: Roughly how many months of runway does the company have at today's burn?
When was the last funding round, and how much was raised?
Is net burn falling as revenue grows, or rising faster than revenue?
Is the company raising because growth needs cash, or because cash is running out?
If you hold ESOPs, how many shares do they represent, and out of how many in total? (Chapter 3 shows why this matters.)

body.title: Spot the strongest reason
body.question: Which of these is the strongest reason for a startup to raise outside capital?
options: Three competitors announced seed rounds this quarter
The founders want a well-known VC on the cap table for credibility
Its snacks sell out every production batch within a week, and each ₹1 spent on marketing returns ₹3 of gross margin within six months
The product has few paying users, so more marketing money should help it find product-market fit
body.explanation: Proven demand plus a reliable return on growth spending means cash, not customers, is the bottleneck. That is exactly what outside money should fix. Competitor rounds and VC logos are vanity, and spending to find product-market fit amplifies losses rather than solving the real problem.

body.title: The profitable founder gets a term sheet
body.scenario: Kavya runs a Coimbatore B2B software company that helps textile mills plan production. It has ₹6 crore in annual recurring revenue, grows about 35% a year, earns a 20% net margin and has ₹4 crore in the bank. A well-known VC offers ₹20 crore at a ₹100 crore post-money valuation, which is 20% of the company. In return, the VC expects revenue to roughly triple in two years and wants a board seat.
body.prompt: Should Kavya take the money? What does she need to figure out before deciding?
body.modelAnswer:
Not automatically. She is default alive, profitable and self-funding, so she can negotiate from strength or walk away.
1. Is growth limited by cash or by demand? If mills are queuing up and she cannot hire implementation staff fast enough, capital helps. If sales are slow because the market is small, ₹20 crore will not create customers.
2. Is the market big enough for a venture-scale outcome? Tripling revenue to about ₹18 crore in two years needs many more mills, likely new geographies such as Bangladesh or Vietnam.
3. What does staying bootstrapped look like? At 35% a year with no dilution, ₹6 crore of revenue becomes roughly ₹27 crore in five years, and she keeps 100% of it.
4. What is she really giving up? 20% of the company, a board seat and the freedom to grow at her own pace.
If the answers to 1 and 2 are a clear yes, the round can accelerate a much bigger outcome. If not, she should stay bootstrapped or consider a much smaller raise tied to a specific growth plan.

body.title: The key number
body.textWithBlank: Cash in the bank divided by monthly net burn gives a startup's ___.
body.explanation: Runway tells you how many months the company can survive at its current burn. It decides when a startup must start raising, and how much negotiating power it has when it does.

cards.definition: Monthly cash expenses minus monthly cash revenue: how much cash the company loses each month.
Cash in bank divided by monthly net burn: the number of months before cash runs out.
Building a company using founders' own money and the business's cash flow, without outside equity investors.
The point at which customers clearly want the product, buy it, return and recommend it.
The fall in existing shareholders' ownership percentage when new shares are issued.
A startup that will reach profitability on its current growth and costs before its cash runs out.

points: Raising money is a trade, not an achievement: you give up ownership, control and freedom in exchange for speed.
Runway equals cash divided by monthly net burn. Start raising with 12 to 18 months left, because a round often takes three to six months.
Good reasons to raise: growth limited by cash rather than demand, winner-take-most markets, heavy upfront investment and long sales cycles.
Bad reasons to raise: peer pressure, validation, flattering valuations, hunting for product-market fit by spending and avoiding fixes to broken economics.
Dilution is priced today but paid at exit. 20% sold for ₹2 crore is worth ₹40 crore if the company later sells for ₹200 crore.
Zerodha and Zoho show bootstrapping can build very large companies. Dunzo shows that raising large amounts does not guarantee a working business.
Runway and funding decisions affect hiring, increments and ESOP value, so employees, HR and finance teams should read these signals too.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment, legal or financial advice. Company figures are based on public reports and may be revised. The Bengaluru, Pune, Jaipur and Coimbatore companies in the examples and exercises, including Kavya's, are illustrative. Speak to a qualified professional before making funding decisions for your company.
